newsitem.title: ITALY: Economist Milton Friedman says single currency "a bad idea".
newsitem.headline: Economist Milton Friedman says single currency "a bad idea".

text.p: European nations will have a tough time making their planned single currency work because their economies are not flexible enough to cope with unexpected shocks, Nobel Prize-winning economist Milton Friedman said.
The U.S. economist was quoted in the news magazine Panorama as saying that the planned currency, the euro, was "a bad idea."
Friedman, who won the Nobel prize for economics in 1976, popularized free-market ideas that influenced former President Ronald Reagan and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s.

For a currency union to work "you need countries which are relatively homogeneous in their economic structure and able to respond in the same way to any shocks, those chance effects which influence an economy," Friedman was quoted as saying.
"The various countries which are getting ready to enter the euro do not have these characteristics in common."
He said it would be better for political union to take shape before a monetary union went ahead.
"In Europe, countries are politically independent and each one speaks a different language. There is no single labor market and there is limited mobility between one country and another," he said.
European countries would find it much easier to create a single market and abolish trade barriers with flexible exchange rates rather than in a currency union.
He said if Italy were part of a currency union it would be hard if some big problem hit it harder than other countries in the region.
"How could Italy react? With the euro the only way is deflation, that is lowering prices and favoring a depression."
Flexible exchange rates would give countries more room to maneuver, he added.
